CS001.problem: By 1900 mathematicians had grown confident that every theorem could be derived from a few self-evident starting points. Then paradoxes appeared in the foundations. Bertrand Russell’s, found in 1901, showed that the innocent-sounding idea of “the collection of all collections that do not contain themselves” contradicts itself. If the foundations could produce contradictions, everything built on them was suspect. Gottlob Frege had tried to derive arithmetic from pure logic, and Russell’s paradox seemed to wreck his system. Mathematics needed foundations it could trust, and a way to check that trust.
CS001.insight: Alfred North Whitehead and Russell rebuilt mathematics from the ground up in a fully symbolic language, where every step is written out and justified by an explicit rule rather than by intuition. To block the paradox they sorted everything into a hierarchy of “types”: a collection may only contain things of a lower type than itself, so nothing can contain itself. Then, over three volumes, they derived the properties of numbers and much else from logic alone. The lasting point was less any single proof than the demonstration that proof itself can be treated as the manipulation of symbols.
CS001.analogy: It is the difference between explaining a recipe in words and writing it so exactly that a robot with no sense of taste could follow it. Nothing is left to judgment; only the rules decide.
CS001.unlocked: Treating proof as mechanical symbol manipulation made a new kind of object available for study: the formal system. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are about a system of exactly this kind, and Church and Turing’s definitions of computation grew from asking what it means to follow rules mechanically. McCulloch and Pitts borrowed its logical notation to describe neurons. In 1956 the Logic Theorist, an early AI program, proved theorems from Principia’s second chapter, and the ideal of fully explicit derivations is the distant ancestor of today’s proof assistants and automated reasoning tools.
CS001.left_open: The system was vast and clumsy: the proof that 1 + 1 = 2 arrives hundreds of pages in. Some of its axioms, such as the axiom of infinity, did not look purely logical. Above all, the hope that the system could settle every mathematical question was a promise, not a proven fact. Whether any such complete and trustworthy system could exist was exactly what Kurt Gödel would answer two decades later.
CS001.diagram_alt: A four-layer stack: axioms of logic and rules at the base, then the theory of types, then classes and numbers, then arithmetic and analysis at the top, with the note that 1 + 1 = 2 is proved hundreds of pages in.
review: Logic Theorist proved theorems from Principia chapter 2 (Newell, Simon and Shaw, 1956)
McCulloch and Pitts cite Principia (edge E008)
Frege's system was undermined by Russell's paradox (1901-02) (edge E001)

CS002.problem: David Hilbert had set mathematicians a goal: place mathematics on a permanently secure footing. The recipe was to write down a formal system like Principia’s and then prove, by simple finite reasoning, that it is consistent (it never proves a falsehood) and complete (every statement is either provable or refutable). Principia had supplied the kind of system; what remained was the proof that it behaved. Many expected this to be a matter of time and effort rather than a matter of principle.
CS002.insight: Gödel noticed that statements about formulas and proofs can be turned into statements about numbers, by giving every symbol, formula and proof a numeric code. This is now called Gödel numbering. Once a system can talk about numbers, it can indirectly talk about itself. He constructed a sentence which, once decoded, says “this sentence is not provable in this system.” If the system proves it, the system proves something false. If it does not, the sentence is true but unprovable. So any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic must contain true statements it cannot prove. His second theorem added that such a system cannot prove its own consistency.
CS002.analogy: It is a cousin of the liar paradox, “this statement is false,” with truth swapped for provability. That small change turns a paradox into a theorem: the system’s own machinery for certifying statements cannot certify this one.
CS002.unlocked: It ended Hilbert’s programme in its original form. For computing, its method mattered as much as its conclusion. Encoding programs, proofs and statements as data is exactly the move Turing and Church would make, and it is the same idea that lets one program read, run or analyse another. Gödel also used primitive recursive functions, an early precise class of calculable functions, which pointed toward a mathematical definition of computation. Verification and program analysis still live with its consequence: no fixed method can prove everything that is true.
CS002.left_open: Gödel’s theorems were about provability inside particular formal systems. They did not say what a “mechanical procedure” is in general; that notion was still informal. And a sharper question remained: even if we cannot prove everything, could some mechanical method at least decide which statements are provable? That was Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem, and it stayed open until 1936.
CS002.diagram_alt: A sentence G says 'the formula numbered n is not provable', where n is G's own Gödel number. A loop shows G talks about itself. Two outcomes: if provable the system proves a falsehood; if not provable, G is true but unprovable.
review: Gödel's section 4 states the results do not contradict Hilbert's formalist viewpoint (basis for tagging E003 explicit)
Turing's paper cites Gödel (basis for tagging E005 explicit)

CS003.problem: After Gödel, the question shifted from “can everything be proved?” to “can we at least decide, mechanically, what is provable?” Answering it needed a precise definition of “mechanical procedure.” Without one, nobody could prove that no such procedure exists. Words like algorithm or effective calculation were intuitions, not definitions, and a proof of impossibility needs something exact to be impossible about. Mathematicians had many examples of calculations but no agreed boundary around the idea.
CS003.insight: Alonzo Church proposed that “effectively calculable” should mean what can be expressed in his lambda calculus, a tiny language in which everything is a function. It has just two moves: create a function, and apply a function to an argument. Numbers, arithmetic, logic and repetition can all be encoded as functions. With this definition he proved that some problems, such as deciding whether two lambda expressions are equivalent, cannot be solved by any calculation. He also showed that lambda-definable functions match Gödel and Herbrand’s general recursive functions, which suggested the definition captured something natural. The claim that this really is what “calculable” means is now called Church’s thesis.
CS003.analogy: Imagine building all of programming from a single move: write a recipe with a blank in it (“take x and do this to it”), then plug something into the blank. Counting, choosing and repeating are all made by plugging recipes into recipes.
CS003.unlocked: Church gave the first precise answer to “what is computation?” and the first example of a problem no computation can solve. His notation became the root of functional programming: LISP borrowed it directly, and its descendants (ML, Haskell, and the lambda expressions in modern Python, JavaScript and Java) carry it forward. It also gave programming-language theory a way to say what a program means, by treating computation as the step-by-step simplification of expressions, an idea that still underlies how languages are specified and compilers reason about code.
CS003.left_open: Many logicians were not convinced that function substitution captured everything a human calculator does. A language of nested substitution does not obviously resemble working through a calculation on paper. The definition needed independent support, and it arrived within months from Alan Turing, who started from a very different picture: a machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape.
CS003.diagram_alt: A function (lambda x. x + 1) applied to 2 reduces to 2 + 1 and then to 3. Below, three boxes joined by equals signs: lambda-definable, Turing-computable and general recursive functions are the same class.
review: Church's 1936 paper cites Gödel and uses Gödel's arithmetization (basis for E004 explicit)
McCarthy 1960 cites Church's lambda notation (basis for E022 explicit)
Equivalence of lambda-definable and general recursive functions was shown by Church/Kleene around 1935-36

CS004.problem: Church had a definition of effective calculation, but it felt arbitrary. Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem asked for a mechanical procedure that decides whether any statement of logic is provable. To show no such procedure exists, one needed a definition of “mechanical” so obviously right that nobody could argue the procedure had been defined too narrowly. What was missing was a picture of calculation that people would accept at a glance.
CS004.insight: Turing started from what a human calculator does: work on paper, look at one symbol at a time, keep a limited amount in mind, and write or change marks. Stripped to essentials, that is a tape divided into cells, a head that reads and writes one symbol at a time, and a finite table of rules. This is a Turing machine. He then made two leaps. First, a single “universal” machine can read the description of any other machine from its tape and imitate it, so one machine can perform every computation: programs are data. Second, a diagonal argument shows that no machine can decide, for every machine, a question closely related to whether it will ever stop. Hence the Entscheidungsproblem has no solution. Turing also showed his machines compute exactly what Church’s lambda calculus does.
CS004.analogy: A record player is one device that plays any record, because the music is on the disc, not in the machine. The universal machine is the same trick for computation: the “disc” is a description of what to compute.
CS004.unlocked: The paper fixed the meaning of “computable,” proved the first limits of computation, and in the universal machine foreshadowed the general-purpose computer, the stored program, interpreters and compilers. It gave later computer science its standard model: complexity theory counts steps of Turing machines, and Turing returned to the machine picture in 1950 to ask whether machines can think. That Church’s and Turing’s independent definitions turned out to agree is the main reason the Church–Turing thesis is trusted.
CS004.left_open: A Turing machine says what is computable in principle, not what is computable efficiently or in reasonable time. It is a mathematical idealisation with an endless tape, not a blueprint for building a machine. And the Church–Turing thesis can never be proved, because “effectively calculable” is an informal idea. Questions of cost, how many steps and how much memory, would need a new theory.
CS004.diagram_alt: A tape of cells holding symbols, with a read-write head over one cell and a box showing the machine's current state, plus one rule: in state q2 reading 1, write 0, move right, go to state q3.
review: Turing's paper proves an undecidability result for 'circle-free' machines; the halting-problem phrasing came later, so the text says 'closely related to whether it will ever stop'
Equivalence with lambda-definability was shown in Turing's 1937 follow-up and a note appended to the paper

CS005.problem: Telephone exchanges and early automatic machines were built from thousands of relays, electromagnetic switches that are either open or closed. Engineers designed these circuits by intuition, sketches and trial and error. There was no systematic way to know that a circuit did what was intended, or whether a simpler one would do the same job. As networks of switches grew, design by hand became unmanageable. A single wiring mistake in such a tangle was hard to find, and every redundant switch cost money.
CS005.insight: Claude Shannon, then a master’s student at MIT, noticed that a switch has two states, just as a statement in George Boole’s algebra of logic is either true or false. Two switches in series let current through only if both are closed, which is AND. Two in parallel let current through if either is closed, which is OR. A contact that is closed when its relay is off acts as NOT. So any circuit can be written as a Boolean expression, simplified with algebra, and rebuilt in a cheaper form; and any logical statement can be wired up as a circuit that computes it.
CS005.analogy: Picture two doors in a corridor: to get through you need both open (AND). Picture two alternative corridors: you get through if either is open (OR). Shannon saw that the plumbing of switches and the algebra of logic are the same thing, so simplifying one simplifies the other.
CS005.unlocked: This is the foundation of digital circuit design. Logic gates, adders and control units follow from the correspondence, and so does the practice of minimising circuits by algebra. It tied abstract logic to physical machines: whether built from relays, vacuum tubes or transistors, a computer’s logic is Boolean. Designers of the first stored-program computers used this style of reasoning, and it remains the language in which chip designers describe hardware today.
CS005.left_open: The thesis treated circuits as pure logic, with the output fixed by the current inputs. It said little about memory, timing, or how to organise switches into a whole computer: that needed an architecture. And it said nothing yet about what travels through circuits. Shannon himself would take that up a decade later by asking how much information a signal carries.
CS005.diagram_alt: Two switches A and B in series on one wire (current flows only if both are closed, AND) and in parallel on two branches (current flows if either is closed, OR), with a key stating series is AND, parallel is OR and a normally closed contact is NOT.
review: Shannon's paper builds on Boole; the thesis is from 1937, the journal paper 1938 (basis for E010 explicit)

CS006.problem: Brains are made of neurons that either fire or do not, yet thought seems limitless and abstract. In the early 1940s no one had a precise way to say how a network of simple cells could compute anything, let alone reason. Neuroscience and logic spoke separate languages, and it was unclear whether the mind could be explained by the first at all.
CS006.insight: Warren McCulloch, a neurophysiologist, and Walter Pitts, a young logician, proposed a deliberately simplified neuron. It receives signals from other neurons and fires only if enough excitatory inputs arrive and no inhibitory input blocks it. Wire several together and they behave like AND, OR and NOT gates. They argued that any logical expression can be realised by a suitably wired network, and that networks given a tape to read and write could compute anything a Turing machine can. On this picture the brain is a computing device, and the mind’s operations are logical ones. Concretely, a neuron that needs both of two inputs to fire computes AND, one that needs either computes OR, and one that an inhibitory signal can silence gives NOT.
CS006.analogy: A neuron is a committee that votes: it acts if enough members say yes and nobody uses a veto. Chain committees together and you can compute any yes-or-no decision.
CS006.unlocked: This was the first mathematical model of a neural network, and it started the line of work that leads through Rosenblatt’s perceptron to modern deep learning. It also made “the mind as computation” a research claim. John von Neumann borrowed the idealised neuron as the basic building block in his EDVAC design, and the Dartmouth proposal listed neuron nets among its research topics. The idea that simple units wired together can compute anything remains the premise of every neural network today.
CS006.left_open: The model neurons had fixed connections and thresholds, so the network could not learn. Real neurons are far messier than on-off switches. How a network might adjust its own connections from experience, which is what makes brains, and later machines, flexible, was left untouched. It would take Hebb’s ideas, the perceptron, and eventually backpropagation to address it.
CS006.diagram_alt: Two input neurons feed one model neuron through connections of weight 1. The neuron fires if its summed input reaches a threshold of 2, which makes it an AND gate. A third input can veto firing.
review: McCulloch and Pitts cite Principia, Carnap, Hilbert and Ackermann, and Turing (basis for E008 and E009 explicit)
Von Neumann's First Draft cites McCulloch and Pitts (basis for E013 explicit)
Dartmouth proposal names Pitts and McCulloch among those who worked on neuron nets (E018)

CS007.problem: Early electronic computers such as ENIAC were fast, but programming them meant physically rewiring cables and setting switches, which could take days. Memory was scarce and expensive. As the Moore School team planned a successor, they needed a clean design for a general-purpose machine whose task could be changed quickly, and a way to describe that design without tying it to one kind of electronic component.
CS007.insight: John von Neumann’s report described a machine of a few functional parts: a central arithmetic unit, a central control unit, a memory, and input and output. The crucial choice was a single memory holding both the data and the instructions, all encoded as numbers. A program could then be loaded like data, changed while running, and executed from memory one instruction after another. The report also described the machine’s logic organs as idealised neurons in the style of McCulloch and Pitts, which let the design be reasoned about without committing to a particular electronic technology.
CS007.analogy: Imagine a kitchen where recipe cards and ingredients sit on the same shelves. The cook can fetch a card just as easily as a carrot, and can even rewrite a card in the middle of cooking. That shared shelf is the stored program.
CS007.unlocked: The “von Neumann architecture” is still how nearly every computer is organised. Because programs are data, software could be separate from hardware, which made assemblers, compilers and operating systems possible, and so an entire software industry. A machine that could be reprogrammed in minutes instead of days turned computers from special-purpose calculators into general tools, the practical counterpart of Turing’s universal machine. Within a few years, working stored-program machines such as the Manchester Baby (1948) and EDSAC in Cambridge (1949) proved the idea in practice.
CS007.left_open: A single path between processor and memory becomes a bottleneck, and the design is inherently sequential. The report was an unfinished draft, circulated under one name, and who deserved credit for the ideas was disputed. Most pressing for users, programs still had to be written as numeric machine instructions by hand, a laborious and error-prone task that motivated the first high-level languages.
CS007.diagram_alt: A control unit and an arithmetic unit connected to a single memory that holds both instructions and data as numbers, with input and output devices attached to the memory.
review: First Draft cites McCulloch and Pitts for its idealised neuron elements (basis for E013 explicit)
Whether von Neumann drew directly on Turing's universal machine is debated; E014 is tagged interpretive and says so
Credit dispute: Eckert and Mauchly vs von Neumann as sole author of the draft
Manchester Baby ran the first stored program in 1948; EDSAC entered service in 1949

CS008.problem: Telephone, telegraph and radio engineers thought in terms of voltages, bandwidth and signal strength. There was no way to say how much information a message contains, or what the best possible rate of reliable communication over a noisy line is. Many believed that noise forced a bargain: the more reliable you wanted the message, the slower you had to send it, with perfect reliability costing infinite time.
CS008.insight: Claude Shannon defined information by surprise: the less likely a message, the more information it carries. Counted in bits, the average information of a source is its entropy, and the meaning of the message is irrelevant to the engineering problem. He then proved two surprising results. A source can be compressed to about its entropy but no further. And every noisy channel has a capacity: below it, suitable codes make errors as rare as you like without slowing the rate toward zero. He framed all communication the same way: source, encoder, noisy channel, decoder, destination. A fair coin toss carries exactly one bit; a coin that lands heads nine times in ten carries less, because its outcome is less surprising.
CS008.analogy: In the game of twenty questions, each well-chosen yes-or-no answer is one bit. Entropy is roughly how many questions you need on average to identify the message, and the channel capacity is how many questions’ worth of answers can get across despite a noisy phone line.
CS008.unlocked: Shannon’s theory underlies data compression (ZIP, JPEG, MP3), error-correcting codes (compact discs, deep-space links, Wi-Fi and mobile networks), and the whole idea of digital communication. It made the bit the unit of information and brought a statistical view of messages that spread to linguistics, biology, cryptography and machine learning. Chomsky’s study of language began by pushing against its statistical models of text.
CS008.left_open: Shannon proved that good codes exist without saying how to build practical ones. It took decades of work, from Hamming and Reed–Solomon to turbo and LDPC codes, to approach capacity. And his information is about symbols, not significance: the theory deliberately ignores what a message means, so it says nothing about meaning, relevance or understanding.
CS008.diagram_alt: A communication chain: source, encoder, noisy channel with a noise source feeding in, decoder, destination. Below, three notes: entropy H is the average information in bits, a source can be compressed to about H, and reliable communication is possible below channel capacity C.
review: E012 (CS005 to CS008) is interpretive: it reads Shannon's move from binary switches to binary information as one line of thought

CS009.problem: By 1950 digital computers existed, and people argued about whether machines could think. The arguments tended to dissolve into disagreements about the word “think,” on which nobody agreed. Turing wanted a question that could be tested rather than endlessly debated, and he wanted to show that the arguments against machine intelligence were weaker than they looked.
CS009.insight: Turing replaced “Can machines think?” with a game. An interrogator exchanges typed messages with two hidden players, one human and one machine, and must decide which is which. If the machine can fool the interrogator often enough, we have no good grounds to deny it intelligence. This “imitation game,” now called the Turing test, turns a philosophical question into an empirical one. He then worked through objections: theological, mathematical (citing Gödel), the claim that machines can only do what they are told, and more. And he sketched a route to success: not programming an adult mind but building a “child machine” and educating it, so that learning is central. He predicted that by about the year 2000 an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 per cent chance of identifying the machine after five minutes of questioning.
CS009.analogy: It is a blind taste test. Instead of arguing about whether a wine is “really” a Burgundy, you ask whether experts can tell it from one when they cannot see the label.
CS009.unlocked: The paper made machine intelligence a respectable research goal and gave the field a recognisable benchmark. Its objections section anticipated many later debates, such as Searle’s Chinese room, and its “child machine” passage is an early statement of machine learning. It also drew directly on his own universal machine: because a digital computer can imitate any other machine, a computer with the right program could in principle imitate a mind.
CS009.left_open: The test measures conversation, and arguably only imitation: a program tuned to fool judges can pass without understanding anything. The paper offered no concrete method for building such a machine and no organised research programme. That came a few years later, when a small group chose a name and an agenda for the new field. Critics also point out that the test rewards deception and conversational tricks, which is why later researchers have proposed harder, more specific benchmarks.
CS009.diagram_alt: An interrogator on the left sends typed questions to two hidden players, A and B, on the right, separated by a screen. One player is a human and one is a machine. The question is whether the interrogator can tell which is which.
review: Turing 1950 argues from universality of digital computers (basis for E016 explicit)
E017 (CS009 to CS010) is interpretive; the Dartmouth proposal does not cite Turing
Turing predicted a 30% chance of fooling an interrogator after 5 minutes by about 2000

CS010.problem: In the early 1950s, work related to machine intelligence was scattered across several fields: cybernetics, automata theory, information theory, neural networks, computer chess. It had no common name, no shared agenda and no community. Researchers in different fields rarely met, and each used different vocabulary for similar ideas. Nobody had yet said, in one place, what a unified effort would try to do. The organisers themselves came from these separate strands: Shannon had written on programming a computer to play chess, and Minsky had built a neural-network learning machine as a student.
CS010.insight: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote to the Rockefeller Foundation asking for support for a two-month summer study at Dartmouth College in 1956. The key sentence is a conjecture: every aspect of learning, or any other feature of intelligence, can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it. They listed topics to study, including programming languages, neuron nets, the size of computations, self-improvement, abstraction, and randomness and creativity. The proposal also gave the field its name: “artificial intelligence.”
CS010.analogy: It works like a founding charter. A scattered group of researchers with similar questions gets a name, a banner and a list of problems, the way naming a conference “genomics” could turn many separate labs into one field.
CS010.unlocked: Artificial intelligence became an academic field, with labs at MIT, Stanford and Carnegie Mellon and a stream of funding. The workshop itself featured Newell and Simon’s Logic Theorist, and McCarthy went on to create LISP as a language for the field’s symbolic programs. The conjecture set the agenda for decades of symbolic AI: represent knowledge explicitly, then search and reason over it. The name itself stuck, even though some of the participants disliked it.
CS010.left_open: The proposal assumed that a small group could make significant progress in a single summer, which was wildly optimistic. It set out topics but no method, and soon the field split between symbolic reasoning and neural networks. Repeated cycles of overpromising and disappointment, later called AI winters, followed. The conjecture itself remains unproven: nobody has shown that every aspect of intelligence can be so precisely described.
CS010.diagram_alt: A central circle labelled 'simulate intelligence on a machine' with seven spokes to the proposal's topics: automatic computers, programming languages, neuron nets, size of a computation, self-improvement, abstractions, and randomness and creativity.
review: McCarthy has said he chose 'artificial intelligence' partly to distance the field from cybernetics (basis for ghost G005 and edge E019, tagged interpretive)
Newell and Simon presented the Logic Theorist at the Dartmouth workshop
Proposal names Pitts and McCulloch among neuron-net workers (E018)
Seven topics in the proposal: verify list against the original text
IPL (Newell/Simon list-processing language) preceded LISP; Minsky built a neural learning machine (SNARC) as a student; Shannon wrote on computer chess (1950)

CS011.problem: Linguists mostly catalogued the forms of languages. Shannon’s information theory had suggested a different idea: treat language as a statistical source in which each word depends on the few words before it. But nobody had a mathematically precise way to ask what kind of machinery a grammar of English requires, or to compare the power of different ways of writing grammars.
CS011.insight: Noam Chomsky compared three ways of describing a language. In finite-state (Markov) models, the next word depends on a bounded past. In phrase-structure grammars, rewriting rules such as S → NP VP build sentences from nested phrases. Transformational grammars add rules that rearrange those phrase structures. He argued that finite-state models cannot generate English, because sentences nest dependencies, such as “if… then” inside “either… or,” and matching them needs unbounded memory of what is still open. Phrase-structure rules can express nesting. In 1959 he organised grammars into the hierarchy now taught in computer science, whose levels match types of machine, from finite automata up to Turing machines.
CS011.analogy: Think of checking parentheses. A machine that remembers only the last symbol cannot tell whether every opening bracket gets a matching closer. You need a stack of what is currently open, and that extra memory is what separates the levels of the hierarchy.
CS011.unlocked: Chomsky’s work founded formal language theory, linking grammars to automata and giving computer science the tools to describe programming languages precisely. Context-free grammars became the standard way to specify syntax, and parsers and compilers are built directly from them. It also reshaped linguistics and the early study of language by computer, and its machine-matched levels remain a staple of the first course in the theory of computation. Pushdown automata and regular expressions, tools programmers use daily, correspond to levels of this hierarchy.
CS011.left_open: Whether natural languages are really context-free, and how a child or a machine could learn a grammar from examples, stayed controversial. When speech recognition and machine translation finally succeeded in the 1980s and after, it was largely with statistical methods, the approach this paper had argued against. The neat generative picture and the data-driven one remained in tension.
CS011.diagram_alt: On the left, nested boxes: finite-state models inside phrase-structure grammars, with transformations as a further layer. On the right, the words 'if either A or B then C' with arcs pairing if with then and either with or, showing nesting that needs memory.
review: The 1956 paper compares three models; the four-level hierarchy was formalised in Chomsky 1959 (the node's short label was changed from 'Chomsky hierarchy' to 'Three models of language' for this reason)
Chomsky 1956 discusses Shannon-style Markov models of language (basis for E020 explicit)
Statistical methods dominating speech recognition and translation from the 1980s

CS012.problem: Programming early computers meant writing instructions one machine operation at a time, in numeric codes or assembly language. It was slow, error-prone and tied to one machine, and the cost of programming often rivalled the cost of the computer. Many experts believed an automatic translator from mathematical notation would produce code so slow that nobody would use it: machines were scarce and programmers took pride in hand-tuned code. Programmers also had to track where each number lived in memory, so rewriting a program for a new machine meant starting again.
CS012.insight: John Backus’s team at IBM designed a language in which scientists write formulas almost as they do in mathematics, with loops and conditions, and a compiler translates them into machine code. The real achievement was making the compiler good enough to win over sceptics. The team put much of their effort into optimisation, such as choosing registers wisely and avoiding repeated calculations, so the generated code ran nearly as fast as code written by hand. The system was delivered for the IBM 704 in 1957, after years of work.
CS012.analogy: It is like ordering a meal by naming the dish instead of describing each knife stroke to the cook. That only works if the cook is good enough that you do not miss your own instructions.
CS012.unlocked: FORTRAN proved that high-level languages could be efficient, which made them the default. It launched compiler construction as a discipline, with parsing, optimisation and code generation. Scientists and engineers could now write their own programs, and the language is still used today in scientific computing, such as weather and climate models and physics simulations. Every later language had to answer the question FORTRAN settled: it is possible to be both convenient and fast.
CS012.left_open: FORTRAN’s design was shaped by one machine and by numerical work. It had awkward control structures, leaning on GOTO, and at first no recursion and few ways to organise data beyond arrays. It was also hard to describe formally. Languages with cleaner structure came next, along with Dijkstra’s 1968 case against GOTO, and McCarthy’s LISP took programming in a quite different direction.
CS012.diagram_alt: A formula Y = A*X + B as a scientist writes it enters a compiler that parses, optimises and generates code, and comes out as machine code: load X, multiply by A, add B, store Y.
review: Delivered for the IBM 704 in 1957; the often-quoted team effort (about 18 person-years) was not stated in the text; verify before adding it
E021 (CS007 to CS012) is interpretive

CS013.problem: Given a map of towns joined by roads of different lengths, how do you find the shortest route from one town to another? The obvious method is to check every possible route, but the number of routes explodes as the map grows, beyond what any computer could handle. A usable method needed effort that grows modestly with the size of the map, and a guarantee that its answer really is the shortest.
CS013.insight: Edsger Dijkstra’s method keeps a set of towns whose shortest distance from the start is already known. Repeatedly it takes the nearest town not yet settled and fixes its distance, because no route through any other unsettled town could be shorter, since road lengths are never negative. Then it updates the distance estimates of that town’s neighbours. Each step settles exactly one town, so the work grows roughly with the square of the number of towns instead of exploding. The paper is three pages long; the heart of it is the argument for why the greedy choice is safe, a proof of correctness as much as a procedure. It also gave a method for the cheapest way of connecting all the towns.
CS013.analogy: Think of ripples spreading from a stone dropped in a pond. The water reaches the nearest points first, and once the ripple touches a point you know that is the earliest it can arrive.
CS013.unlocked: Dijkstra’s algorithm became a staple: it sits inside internet routing protocols such as OSPF, in map and navigation software, and in countless planning and optimisation tools. More broadly it showed the style of algorithm design where a clever invariant lets a locally best choice be globally right. Dijkstra himself carried that emphasis on proving correctness into his later work on programming.
CS013.left_open: The method fails if road lengths can be negative, which later algorithms such as Bellman–Ford handle. Its roughly quadratic cost was fine for small maps but not for very large sparse ones, until better data structures reduced it. And the paper had no general way to compare algorithms or say what is fundamentally hard: that needed a theory of computational complexity, which began in the following decade.

CS014.problem: Artificial intelligence research needed programs that manipulate symbols and structures, such as logical formulas, sentences and plans, not just numbers. FORTRAN was built for arithmetic. It had no recursion at first, no easy way to build structures while running, and no way for a program to treat another program as data. Programmers also lacked a clean mathematical account of what a program means. Researchers building the first AI programs were writing them in assembly code or in IPL, a list-processing language that was powerful but low-level.
CS014.insight: John McCarthy defined a tiny language. Data are symbolic expressions: atoms and pairs, which chain into lists. Programs are written as the same kind of expression. A handful of primitive operations (car, cdr, cons, atom, eq), conditional expressions, function definitions using Church’s lambda notation, and recursion are enough to build the rest. He then wrote the language’s own interpreter in the language itself, a function now called eval, a few lines that can run any program given as a list. It is the programming-language counterpart of Turing’s universal machine. To manage memory in a world of freely built lists, the design also introduced automatic garbage collection.
CS014.analogy: Imagine a recipe book whose recipes are written so uniformly that one chapter can teach the cook to read every other chapter, including itself.
CS014.unlocked: LISP became the main language of symbolic AI for three decades, and its ideas spread everywhere: recursion, conditionals as expressions, functions as values, garbage collection, interactive read-eval-print loops and code that writes code. Later dialects such as Scheme became the teaching language of Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, and today’s lambda expressions and metaprogramming in mainstream languages trace back to it. The notation also made it natural to write programs that take programs as input, and symbolic differentiation was one of the first applications.
CS014.left_open: Early LISP was slow and hungry for memory, and ran best on specialised machines. Its original scoping rules caused subtle bugs, and its uniform parenthesised syntax was hard on human readers. The deeper question it served, whether manipulating symbols is enough to produce intelligence, remained open and would divide AI into rival camps.
